title: How To Turn Coworkers Into Friends
summary: The creator explains three strategies to quickly build friendships with coworkers. The main lesson is that by asking feeling-based questions, opening up about yourself first, and remembering personal details, you can form strong bonds quickly.
key_points: Ask better questions by adding feeling words instead of just using basic what and how questions, e.g., 'What are you excited about on the weekend?'
Revealing things about yourself first gives the other person permission to open up and share about their life.
Start off small with things you care about, then family, and then move on to ambitions and goals.
Write down what people share about their daily life in meetings and bring it up later in the week, e.g., 'Hey, how's your cat doing?'
content: If you like tactics like these, follow for more :) Here's how to turn a coworker into friend And the reason I can say this is the one thing I'm really good at is making friends wherever I go and over the last nine and a half years, this is the reason why I've been able to get three promotions back-to-back, or steal people who are working in great jobs in other big companies, but come and work for me because of building good friendships really quickly. So there's three things that you need to do if you want to make people your friend, quick. The first thing that you need to get good at is asking better questions because what most people do is they ask basic questions like what and how. Okay, what are you going to do on the weekend, or how are you going to do this? That is basic. What you want to do is you want to go deeper into the conversation by adding feeling words to your questions. For example, hey, what are you excited about on the weekend? That's going to get a very different response than, hey, what are you doing on the weekend? If you ask what are you doing, they're going to give you a list of, okay, I'm going to do this, this, and this. But if you ask what are you excited about, they're going to tell you, oh, I'm really excited about watching this show, or I'm really excited about going to this one place. If you add a feeling word like excited to your questions, you're going to get other people to talk about their emotions, and the more emotions people share with you, the more they're going to like you. So, add emotional words to your questions. What are you excited about? What do you hate about this topic? What makes you angry about this topic? Add emotional words to your questions, your questions are going to get better responses, which leads me to the second point. You need to get good at revealing things about yourself first. Up till now, in the last nine and a half years, I've almost hired 400 people for my own businesses, and I can tell you, almost no one starts off sharing about their life immediately. So, I have to do it. And because of me taking that first step and being a leader, it gives the other person room to open up. Most people wait for the other person to open up. If you take the first step, it's going to give the other person permission that they can share something personal about their life as well. Start off small, things that you care about, then things about your family, and then maybe move on to things like your ambitions and your goals. If you share first, you'll be amazed on how quickly other people open up to you as well. Which leads me to the last and most important thing that most people never do. Because I had a guy on my team who was incredibly good at what he does, but his communication skills weren't that great. So, I actually sat down with him, gave him a little training, and said, hey, do this with the team next week. All I asked him to do was when the team says something in a meeting, or they bring up something about their life, because we got opportunities to share about our daily life, write down what they said and then ask them about it later in the week. So, when you're actually having a conversation with them, bring that topic up. Hey, how's your cat doing? And then go into work mode. You don't need to spend a lot of time building rapport, you just need to remember the things that people have already said to you. [Text on screen: How To Turn Coworkers Into Friends]
